tldr: We propose KPI, an interactive kernel for physical interaction that receives target force ranges and tracking requirements (contracts) rather than raw stiffness gains from a high-level planner, automatically adapting arm impedance parameters at 100 Hz during contact without modifying the underlying whole-body tracker.
hero_caption: The coordinated system combining a VLM agent and the physical interaction kernel KPI. The high-level agent derives a nominal trajectory and a contract (specifying which axes to track and which axes to bound force on) from geometric features, while the low-level KPI resolves and adapts arm impedance at a 100 Hz contact rate.
overview:
Whole-body tracking for humanoid robots has made tremendous progress, enabling robots to walk and balance smoothly along trajectories generated by human teleoperation or foundation models. However, tasks involving heavy contact with the environment (physical interaction)—such as turning a winch crank, opening a door, or pinching and carrying a heavy box—remain exceptionally difficult. Trajectory information alone cannot fully capture contact forces and kinematic constraints. If contact stiffness gains are fixed beforehand, even a trajectory error of just a few millimeters can generate tens of Newtons of excessive resisting force, causing motor overloads or slipped grasps.

To address this, the authors developed KPI (Kernel for Physical Interaction), a middleware layer inserted between the trajectory source and an unmodified whole-body tracker. The core concept is that instead of specifying concrete numerical stiffness gains, the high-level layer sends a specification of intent—a contract—defining which directions to track and which directions to hold within a specific force range (e.g., $N$ to $M$ Newtons). Based on tracking errors and a wrench estimate, KPI optimizes the arms' stiffness, damping, and nominal reference progression in real time through a fast 100 Hz loop.

Using a real-world Unitree G1 humanoid without wrist force-torque sensors, zero-shot experiments driven by single-sentence natural language instructions from a GPT-based VLM agent demonstrated the hoisting of another humanoid completely off the ground by turning a winch, as well as door opening and box transport tasks, all completed successfully without task-specific code or prior demonstrations. While standard joint PD control and fixed-gain admittance control failed, KPI demonstrates the power of explicitly abstracting and solving for physical interaction parameters.
contributions: Formulating tasks not as concrete gain values, but as contracts specifying per-direction force ranges and tracking requirements, and proposing a framework that jointly optimizes stiffness, damping, reference progression, and feedforward forces online at contact rate.

Achieving high-speed Cartesian impedance control on a commercial humanoid joint PD interface without wrist force-torque sensors by splitting damping into on-driver diagonal terms and host-computed off-diagonal terms, preventing divergence even while walking.

Building an agentic framework where a VLM detects geometric features from RGB-D images and automatically writes and modifies generic motion cores and contracts, demonstrating contact-rich whole-body coordination on physical hardware without task-specific code.

sections.heading: Why choosing gains ahead of time is fatal for humanoids
sections.summary: When a humanoid manipulates constrained environments like a manual winch, traditional methods that fix stiffness beforehand inevitably fail due to tiny geometric errors producing massive forces. This paper introduces KPI, where a high-level planner provides contracts (such as allowable force bands) instead of gains, and an intermediate kernel autonomously adapts arm control parameters at 100 Hz.
sections.details:
Modern humanoids can walk and balance gracefully while following nominal reference trajectories from teleoperation or Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models using a single whole-body tracking policy. However, this generality fundamentally travels only in the trajectory.

Consider having a humanoid turn a manual winch crank. The high-level controller can issue a circular trajectory and a turning speed, but it cannot know the mechanical resistance across varying crank angles, the exact kinematic circle, or how the load will scale. In conventional systems, arm controllers operate with fixed gains set before the task begins. Consequently, a trajectory discrepancy of just a few millimeters against the crank circle turns into tens of Newtons of excessive resisting force. A constrained crank handle requires stiff control along the tangent direction and soft, compliant control along the radial direction—and these directions rotate continuously as the handle turns.

Previously, overcoming this meant either end-to-end reinforcement learning of trajectories and contact responses together in simulation for every single task, or relying on hand-tuned fixed compliance. But on a walking humanoid, only the physical quantities arising at the end-effector contact interface can be trusted. This work argues that trajectory sources should communicate interaction contracts rather than gain values: while the force generated by a given stiffness depends heavily on displacement, a target force range (e.g., 25–40 N) carries invariant physical meaning regardless of displacement.

This is realized by KPI, a promptable kernel positioned between the trajectory source and an unmodified whole-body tracker. The trajectory source simply provides a nominal trajectory alongside a contract defining per-direction force ranges and tracking requirements. At 100 Hz, KPI optimizes impedance stiffness, damping, reference progression rate, and feedforward force. Its modular design requires only centimeter-level nominal trajectories from above and requires zero modifications to the whole-body tracker below.

sections.heading: The crucial distinction between RL-based skills and existing compliance control
sections.summary: Prior humanoid research either trained contact responses end-to-end in simulation for each task or configured compliance parameters prior to task execution. KPI's key novelty lies in closing an online parameter adaptation loop directly from estimated wrenches at contact rate (100 Hz), all while keeping the underlying whole-body tracker completely unmodified.
sections.details:
To place this work in context, it helps to examine related approaches in humanoid control:

- **Whole-body trackers and task policies**:
Humanoid control commonly relies on whole-body tracking policies (such as SONIC) trained on human motion capture data. However, their arm interfaces typically operate as position servos, with no adaptation to contact forces. Performing contact-heavy tasks (like door opening or box carrying) has traditionally required designing task-specific simulation rewards and training specialized policies from scratch. KPI keeps SONIC completely unmodified, treating new physical interactions as contract switches rather than policy retraining.

- **Task specification representations**:
Hybrid position/force control has long defined which axes should follow position and which should track force. KPI builds upon this intuition but evolves it: instead of tracking a single setpoint, it defines force bands (allowable ranges) and explicitly selects which parameter channels (stiffness gains, trajectory progression rate, feedforward force) are permitted to vary to satisfy those bands.

- **Compliance control in humanoids**:
Prior efforts in humanoid compliance (such as CHIP or MCC) set stiffness values manually before contact or kept them fixed. MCC estimates end-effector wrenches sensorlessly from motor currents for admittance control, but its gains remain constant. KPI adopts MCC's wrench estimation approach as a starting point and adds a feedback path that optimizes controller parameters online during contact based on the estimated wrench.

- **Language models and agent systems**:
In Code-as-Policy frameworks where VLMs generate robot control code, models have been prompted to output per-axis stiffness values. However, the inference latency of VLMs (~1 second) cannot handle rapid contact transitions. KPI bridges this timescale gap by having the VLM write abstract contracts, leaving the low-latency 100 Hz loop to be solved locally by the kernel.

sections.heading: Contract-driven online optimization and stabilizing impedance on commercial hardware
sections.summary: KPI formulates stiffness, reference progression, and feedforward forces into a constrained optimization problem solved at 100 Hz based on contact states and contracts. On the physical hardware, actuator communication delays are mitigated by executing local joint damping directly on motor drivers, while a VLM pipeline handles perception, contract drafting, and self-correction.
sections.details:
The approach consists of three distinct layers: contract-driven optimization, physical humanoid implementation, and the VLM agent.

### III-A Contract-Driven Physical Interaction (KPI Formulation)
The parameter space $\Theta$ adapted by KPI comprises Cartesian stiffness $\mathbf{K}_p$, damping $\mathbf{K}_d$, a scaling factor $\boldsymbol{\rho}$ that modulates the progression of the nominal reference trajectory, and a feedforward wrench compensation term $\mathbf{F}_{\mathrm{ff}}$. The kernel observes the current state $\mathbf{s}_t$, which includes Cartesian tracking errors, velocities, and the estimated external wrench $\hat{\mathbf{W}}_t$.

The contract $\sigma$ sent by the high-level planner specifies directions $d_i$, requirements $o_i$ (tracking, compliant, or constrained), force ranges $[f_i^{\min}, f_i^{\max}]$, and allowed parameter adjustment channels $c_i$. At each 100 Hz cycle, KPI solves a constrained optimization problem to find the closest parameters that satisfy these constraints. Along tracking directions, it minimizes deviation between the end-effector and the reference; when significant resistance is encountered, it scales down $\boldsymbol{\rho}$ to slow reference progression, preventing geometric divergence from the constrained physical path.

### III-B Real-Robot Implementation of Impedance Control
The Unitree G1 humanoid used in experiments features quasi-direct drive (QDD) arm actuators with low gear ratios and high backdrivability. The system runs Cartesian impedance control on top of this at 500 Hz.

A primary technical challenge was communication delay. Generating Cartesian damping by streaming torque commands from a host PC caused high-frequency oscillations due to phase lag. To solve this, the authors decomposed the damping torque $-\mathbf{J}^\top \mathbf{K}_d \mathbf{v} = -\mathbf{D}\dot{\mathbf{q}}$: the diagonal components of the joint-space damping matrix $\mathbf{D}$ (local joint terms $D_{ii}$) are executed directly inside the high-speed motor driver loops, while only the off-diagonal coupling terms ($-\mathbf{D}_{\mathrm{off}}\dot{\mathbf{q}}$) are computed and sent as torques from the host PC. This split damping formulation prevents latency-induced instability and enables robust contact compliance. External wrenches are estimated without wrist sensors using motor currents and gearbox efficiency models, achieving an average error below 5 N.

### III-C VLM-Driven Agent Execution
Using RGB-D camera observations, a Detector identifies the target object's 3D position and articulation axes, while an Analyzer synthesizes the nominal trajectory and contract $\sigma$. A Verifier checks kinematics and collision avoidance before execution. If the task stalls, the Verifier flags the issue, prompting the Analyzer to autonomously adjust the contract or trajectory.

sections.heading: From hoisting a full-size robot with a winch to navigating doors and carrying heavy loads
sections.summary: Evaluated on a physical Unitree G1 without wrist sensors across winch operation, door opening and traversal, and bimanual box transport, KPI achieved a 100% success rate across all 15 trials. In contrast, standard joint PD tracking (SONIC) succeeded in 0/15 trials and sensorless admittance control (MCC*) succeeded in only 1/15, demonstrating an overwhelming performance gap.
sections.details:
Experiments evaluated four conditions: the baseline whole-body locomotion controller SONIC with joint PD tracking, an integrated comparison combining MCC admittance control with SONIC (MCC*), KPI with parameter adaptation disabled (KPI-fixed), and the full proposed KPI. All conditions utilized the same GPT foundation model for the VLM agent, executing zero-shot from single natural language instructions without task-specific code.

### IV-A Winch Cranking Operation
A heavy-duty task requiring the humanoid to rotate a crank handle 4 full revolutions to hoist another G1 robot completely off the ground via a cable. Mechanical resistance varies drastically with crank angle and grows monotonically as the suspended load rises.
- **Results**: KPI achieved 4 full rotations in all 5 trials (100% average progress). Meanwhile, SONIC and MCC* managed to grasp the handle but could not complete even half a turn, averaging 20% progress.
- **Failure Analysis**: When resistance surged, KPI detected end-effector lag, autonomously slowed reference trajectory progression, and increased tangential stiffness. By simultaneously bounding forces along the constrained axes, it turned the crank continuously without binding the mechanism or losing foot traction. Under KPI-fixed, the reference trajectory advanced while the hand stalled, pulling the force vector out of alignment with the tangent and causing the arm to reverse and fail.

### IV-B Door Opening and Traversal
A coordinated task requiring the robot to turn a knob to unlatch the door, step backward to pull it open without colliding with the door's swing path, and walk through. The camera cannot view the entire door frame, creating uncertainty in estimating the hinge radius.
- **Results**: KPI successfully opened and traversed the door in all 5 trials. SONIC failed every trial due to excessive latch resistance, while MCC* repeatedly collided with the handle due to wrench estimation noise and lag, succeeding in only 1 trial.

### IV-C Bimanual Box Transport and Load Robustness
The robot pinches the sides of a cardboard box between flat palms, lifts it from a table, turns 180 degrees while crouching, and places it on another table. Due to low friction, applying too little inward force causes drops, while excessive force triggers motor overcurrent or crushes the box.
- **Results**: Under a light payload (0.85 kg), KPI achieved 5/5 successes (100%). Both SONIC and MCC* failed during lifting (20% success) as palm alignment degraded, losing multi-point contact.
- **Ablations and VLM Prompting**: When heavier weights were added inside the box (medium: 1.85 kg, heavy: 3.0 kg), baseline agents prompted to output direct stiffness values selected overly stiff gains (500–600 N/m), triggering motor overload faults. In contrast, the VLM prompted with KPI contracts selected reasonable force ranges ("25–40 N" and "35–50 N"), allowing KPI's online optimization to lift the payloads securely without exceeding motor limits.

### IV-D Whiteboard Writing and Additional Capabilities
In a whiteboard writing experiment tracing the letters "NB", KPI applied appropriate feedforward normal force to produce clean strokes. Furthermore, when combined with teleoperation, KPI supported highly dynamic whole-body contact tasks, including opening drawers as well as kneeling, standing, and running while transporting boxes.

sections.heading: Potential as a general interaction middleware and remaining hurdles
sections.summary: KPI provides a powerful middleware layer enabling contact-rate parameter adaptation without altering the underlying whole-body tracker. Demonstrating that high-level goal contracts alone can coordinate sophisticated physical interactions, it presents an appealing alternative to training specialized task policies.
sections.details:
The most significant takeaway of this paper is that inserting a thin contact mediation kernel (KPI) between high-level intelligence (VLMs or humans) and low-level locomotion (whole-body tracking policies) enables humanoids to solve complex, contact-rich tasks without any task-specific policy training.

Enabling a humanoid to hoist its own weight on a winch, open an unmodeled door, and transport friction-held boxes from a single prompt represents an important milestone toward practical humanoid manipulation.

Nevertheless, KPI does not formulate its own goals; it is strictly an optimization engine designed to fulfill the contract it receives. If a contract is misformulated, the system may stall. Additionally, the wrench estimator relies on a quasi-static model, meaning sharp impact shocks or dynamic walking vibrations raise the noise floor of force estimation. Future integration of joint torque sensors or tactile end-effectors will be essential for extending this approach to more delicate, high-precision assembly tasks.

sections.heading: Appendix: Local predictive modeling and parameter updates without environmental stiffness identification
sections.summary: KPI's optimization avoids online identification of unknown environment stiffness by using a linearized local model anchored to current measurements over a brief 10 ms (100 Hz) horizon. Single-axis adjustments resolve instantly into closed-form solutions, backed by safe fallbacks within computational limits.
sections.details:
The appendix provides mathematical insights explaining how KPI executes rapid, stable online adaptation at 100 Hz without divergence.

The central challenge in predictive contact modeling is that the environment's mechanical stiffness is unknown. Rather than estimating environment parameters, KPI constructs a local linearized model predicting force variations relative to changes in the robot's own control parameters, grounded in the current impedance relation.

- **Immediate Force Variation Prediction**:
Holding the measured end-effector position $\mathbf{x}_t$ and velocity $\mathbf{v}_t$ fixed, the force response to parameter changes $\Delta \theta$ is approximated to first order as $\tilde{f}_i(\theta; \mathbf{s}_t) = \hat{f}_i + \nabla_\theta f_i^\top (\theta - \theta_t)$. Here, the estimated wrench $\hat{\mathbf{W}}_t$ serves as a fixed reference anchor and is excluded from the optimization decision variables.

- **Short-Horizon Tracking Error Prediction**:
For displacement changes $z_i(s)$ induced by parameter updates, KPI looks across a short horizon ($h = 10$ ms) until the next update cycle, applying a damping-dominated approximation where external forces are treated as constant. Under this formulation, the predictive gain term $g_i = \frac{1 - e^{-k_i h / b_i}}{k_i}$ depends solely on the robot's own controller parameters and the time step $h$, completely eliminating dependency on environmental stiffness.

By leveraging these predictive models, the force bounds ($[f^{\min}, f^{\max}]$) and tracking penalties defined in the contract translate into standard quadratic programs (QP) or direct closed-form expressions. When adjusting single-axis stiffness, the value closest to the current gain that satisfies the constraint is computed instantly via clipped analytic solutions. If a requested force band is physically unachievable, the kernel safely clips parameters to the closest boundary within allowable stiffness ranges, guaranteeing hardware stability.

takeaways: The key to mastering contact-rich manipulation lies not in the trajectory alone, but in explicitly communicating contracts (force bands and compliant axes) across the interaction interface.

Without retraining whole-body humanoid tracking policies for each task, a contact-rate middleware that optimizes impedance gains and nominal reference progression at 100 Hz enables zero-shot execution of constrained physical interactions.
Prompting Vision-Language Models to specify target force ranges (in Newtons) produces far more physically sound and safe behaviors than having them output raw stiffness gains (N/m).

On humanoid hardware subject to actuator communication latency, implementing diagonal joint damping directly inside the motor drivers while computing only Cartesian off-diagonal terms on the host PC is crucial for interaction stability.
limitations: Relying on quasi-static force estimation prevents the system from handling high-impulse impacts or regulating fine, delicate forces amid severe walking vibrations.
Without wrist force-torque sensors, force estimation carries an error margin of a few Newtons, necessitating physical torque or tactile sensors for millimeter-level precision insertion tasks.
Because contract formulation and recovery rely on VLM agent reasoning, misspecified contracts or unforeseen mechanical binding can cause the execution pipeline to stall.
